chunks: 385 - Abu Abdillah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man informed me from Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Bilal al-Mahlabi, saying: I heard Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Quluwayh say:

As for Abu Dalf the scribe - may God not forgive him - we knew him to be a blasphemer, then he displayed exaggeration (ghuluw), then he went mad and was chained, then he was released. We never knew him when he appeared in a gathering except that he was ridiculed, and the Shia knew him for only a short time. The community disavows him and whoever points to him and promotes him. We sent someone to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi when it was said that he had made such claims. He denied that and swore an oath, so we accepted that from him. But when he entered Baghdad, he turned to him and distanced himself from the community and was appointed his successor. We had no doubt that he was on his path, so we cursed him and disavowed him, because with us whoever claims the authority after al-Samari (may God have mercy on him) is a disbeliever, evil, misguided, and leading others astray. And with God is the success.

key_terms.أبو بكر البغدادي: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, a successor to Abu Dalf
key_terms.أبو دلف: Abu Dalf, a false claimant to the Imamate
key_terms.الأمرة: Al-Amr, the authority/leadership of the Imam
key_terms.السمرى: Al-Samari, the last of the Four Deputies
key_terms.الغلو: Ghuluw, exaggeration in attributing divine qualities to the Imams
key_terms.كافر منمس: Kafir munmas, a disbeliever who is evil/disavowed

ai.seo_question: Who was Abu Dalf and why did the Shia disavow him?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* chronicles the trajectory of Abu Dalf, a prominent false claimant to the Minor and Major Deputyship, illustrating the community's gradual shift from tentative acceptance to definitive disavowal (*baraa'ah*) as his eccentricities and eventual madness became apparent. It establishes a critical theological criterion in Shia scholarship: any claimant to the Imamate after the death of al-Samari (the last deputy of Imam al-Hasan al-Askari) is considered a misguided disbeliever, reinforcing the doctrine of the Imam's occultation until his return. The narrative underscores the importance of communal consensus and scholarly verification in distinguishing true authority from impostors during the period of the Major Occultation.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: H 385 - Abu Abdullah Muhammad bin Muhammad bin Noman has narrated from Hasan Ibn Bilal Malhabi, saying, I heard Abul Qasim Ja’far Ibn Muhammad Ibn Quluwayh say:

We knew Abu Dalf, the transcriber, may God not forgive him, to be blasphemous. Then he expressed exaggeration about the Imams and then went crazy and was put in chains. Then he was released. He was ridiculed wherever he went. The Shia knew him for a very little time. They are disdainful of him and whoever promotes him. We sent someone to Abu Bakr Baghdadi when it was said that he had made such claims. He denied that and took oaths. So we took him on his word, but when he went to Baghdad, he turned to this person and distanced himself from the community and was appointed his successor. We had no doubt that he was on his path. So we cursed him and denounced him, because we believe that whoever claims this position after Saymoori, is a denier; he is evil, misguided and leads astray.
